The first 1000 days

By: Nicola De Chaud | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
The first 1000 days of life set us up for the rest of our days - science now says it is so!

Unique Selling Point:
cutting edge research into the profound impact of parenting in the first 1000 days and it's implications for society at large.


Summary:
We look at the first 1000 days of a child's life - the tumultuous irreversible development of the brain in ways which are directly linked to parenting and relating styles.

Recent scientific discoveries in brain development are reshaping our understanding of early childhood development. What makes recent findings so compelling are the enduring and largely irreversible ways in which social conditions and ways of relating are biologically woven into the brain in the first 1000 days.

Most of adult mental ability is formed in the first three years of life, and about half of that before birth. There is overwhelming scientific evidence that the parent-child relationship, in particular responsive sensitive care in the early years of a child’s life, is critical to children’s development. The benefits of responsive caregiving are critical to healthy relationships later in life, in language skills and economic productivity in the adult years.

We talk to experts in the field, neurologists, psychologists and early childhood development experts. We track the progress of babies in institutional care and travel with workers who educate women about their infants experience.

The piece is intimate and accessible merging of science and relational care.


Extra Budget Items:
Travel and accommodation to Cape Town with most interviews based in the Cape

Script:


What is in a babies mind? How do babies think? Do they feel as we do? What would it be like experience the world from this perspective?

Graham: Babies absolutely have thoughts and feelings, they can make things happen, they can predict things they have extraordinary capacities to understand the world. Much much more than you think. They understand when someone is being kind, they understand when someone is being aggressive, they can pick up thoughts and feelings. That’s their job. That’s in a babies job description in a way, to work out how safe their environment is.
What’s he think? What’s she feel? In order to survive. So they’ve absolutely got brilliant minds.

Link: Recent scientific discoveries in brain development are reshaping our understanding of early childhood development. Studies show that what happens in the first 1000 days of life is biologically woven into the brain and impacts a lifetime

Neuroscience demonstrates that neural pathways set down in early life are enduring. They remain, hard wired, and largely irreversible.

Graham: So we’re born with all the neurons we’re ever going to have, which is probably about 100 billion. It’s an extraordinary number of neurons, but what is happening in the first couple of years is that the connections between these neurons are forming – so what we call synaptic connections, and they are forming in response to particular kinds of experiences

UK based Child Psychotherapist and author, Graham Music teaches that very early experiences actually shape brain architecture.

Graham: The babies brain, autonomic nervous system, neurochemical system is being programmed and developed in response to the environment it’s in.

What this means is that particular pathways in the brain are activated in response to particular experiences. Good experiences set up strong, complex pathways, bad experiences disrupt important connections in the brain.

Link: Once those pathways are set up, new science is saying there is little chance of rerouting. And all this happens in the first 1000 days.

According to Psychiatrist Dr Anusha Lukshma, we should begin counting those days, long long before birth.

Anusha; The changes the connections whether these are circuits that are weak or strong are actually formed way before that.

Anusha says brain connections begin to form prenatally twice as fast as an adult brain.

Anusha: Think about 100 billion connections per second…. And it really is that time from conception up until 18 months post delivery…

Babies are pretty smart, very early on and in Utero, so during the pregnancy, babies have an automatic physiological system, which allows them to buffer stressful events.

Graham: So literally stress hormones will cross the placenta if the mother is very very stressed and that will change the nervous system of the baby, who’ll be born predisposed to stress

Graham says prenatal stress has been linked to a myriad of later behavioral problems, adolescent depression, anxiety disorders and increased likelihood of autistic symptoms. Human fetuses are real beings who come into the world pre-wired with particular predispositions.

Link: One of those predispositions is that the human brain is prewired to relate.

There is now overwhelming scientific evidence that the parent-child relationship, in particular responsive sensitive care in first 1000 days is critical to brain development.

Katherine: What is fascinating about the first 1000 days is that too a degree, what isn’t in place in those first 1000 days cannot entirely be recovered

Katherine Frost, heads up Ububele an NGO based in Alex which programmes on the first 1000 days

Katherine: Research is showing us that if babies are responded to as people from the very beginning, those are the children that will, that will develop

Ububele care worker, Khosi Kumalo encourages parents to think about their babies thoughts and feelings. She teaches that what a baby really needs is to be understood

Khosi: By us coming to moms just being with them to help them think about these little people

Khozi Sithole teaches new moms, that babies are separate beings, with their own minds and feeling and that what a baby really needs, is to be understood.

Khosi: It’s not just the baby, you feed the baby, change the baby and that’s it. So for somebody who doesn’t know you kind of make them aware that ‘did you know that when you smile to your baby it does something to them on the inside’, without getting technical and thinking about neurons.

Khosi encourages caregivers to respond sensitively to their babies attempts to connect with them.

Claire: So when a child does not get that sensitive care, how does that change the brain architecture of that child.

Katherine: So the brain is use depended, there are areas of brain they have potential to grow and be used, if they aren’t used, they atrophy – they fall away.

LINK: It’s a case of ‘use it, or lose it”. Neural pathways, much like taxi routes, will simply be discontinued if there is no demand for them.

Graham: We’ve known about this idea that cells that fire together wire together, we’ve known that as a basic idea since the 1950 or so…

However Graham says, the nuts and bolts of it have become clear through sophisticated forms of brain scans.

Graham: We can actually see changes taking place in the brain and we can see which part of the brain are activated in what kind of circumstances in what kind of children. So we can see for example children who have suffered maltreatment, the parts of the brain involved in self reflection, empathy self regulation, calm, they go offline and other more subcortical more primitive parts of the brain involved in aggression, threat, danger will be much more activated.

Babies who have been traumatized, or regularly overwhelmed will grow up with default pathways primed to react.

Graham: which will stop them concentrating, stop them relaxing, stop them learning, stop them being curious, stop them being kind and interested in other people. These are the kids who are very reactive and for example in school get into fights

They are hard wired to be on high alert.

Graham: These are often the kids that end up in the criminal justice system, excluded from school.

Anusha: And I want to make the point that this is not just about people who abuse children in ways that we commonly think. This is also about children growing up in an environment with constant negative reinforcement.

Graham: And whats a bit shocking is how much stress and trauma and abuse there is in so called ordinary families as well. So what we want to do is try to increase capacities for resilience.

Blanche Resant works with families to do just that. Many of the mothers she works with live in stressful challenging environments.

Blanche: and we have to be aware of that and be able to center mom and say to her ‘you are doing good enough work with what you doing, how can we come alongside you to support you better’.

Blanche says mothers mental health is critical to healthy brain development.

Blanche: If a mother is depressed she has a very somber state, she doesn’t respond very easily. A baby will gurgle and giggle and mom will just carry on and babies brain pathway will then take another format to say, whether I smile or whether I gurgle nobodies going to come, nobodies going to respond to me,

An experiment first conducted in the 1970’s demonstrates how sensitive babies are to loss of contact. In the still face experiment, mothers were instructed to become unresponsive to their babies after a short period of play.

Upsound

Anusha: Physically the baby makes more exaggerated attempts to connect. At an emotional level a baby starts to almost deregulate. They become as a lay person would say, this baby is so difficult, what a fussy baby.

Upsound

Anusha: or the reverse might happen if they have repeated episodes where nobody is noticing them, they become very withdrawn. And in fact we worry more about the withdrawn child.



A well known study of Romanian orphans held in appalling conditions in the late 80’s yielded some of the most groundbreaking data about neglect and the developing brain

Graham: Absolutely devastating, shocking, you can see it in their eyes you can see it in their bodies, in their faces, and in their brain you find that many different areas of the brain just didn’t develop in the way that you would hope a childs brain would develop

Anusha: They had differences in their brain capacity in their physical size – so their brains were smaller

Graham: parts of the brain involved in empathy emotion regulation were much less activated

Deprived of human connection, large parts of the prefrontal cortex in the institutionalized children simply did not develop.

Katherine: Where you’ll see big black holes in the brains of children that had inconsistent or absent caregiving in the first 1000 days.

What the study found, is that those children who were removed from the orphanage before the age of two made good progress…

Graham: All kinds of remediation happened in their brain pathways that didn’t happen in the kids who were left behind

Those who were adopted after the age of two, never fully recovered.

Graham: the research that’s being done now found that if you adopt early enough, there’s all kinds of changes that take place, that don’t take place in the kids that remain in the orphanages.

Anusha: What the research does say is that the earlier you correct things the better it is,

For those working with babies in communities, the science is borne out in behavior.

Blanche:. When we see it in reality, we can actually see the long term result is that prevention is much better if you start early.


Experts in the field all agree that the mitigating factor for healthy brain development in all environments is for parents to understand the emotional needs of their children.
Claire: is that always the case
Katherine: That is always the case

What science is now saying quite simply is that love really matters.

Graham: It’s not all touchy feely at all, what we talking about is hard scientific evidence for the profound effect of good and bad experiences on the brain on the body on the health outcomes on the cost to society generally.

Different experiences steer development down different trajectories.

And the brain will form very very different pathways depending on the kind of experiences we have. Because we are a species that learns and adapts to whatever environment we happen to be born into.

metadata.Summary: We look at the first 1000 days of a child's life - the tumultuous irreversible development of the brain in ways which are directly linked to parenting and relating styles. Recent scientific discoveries in brain development are reshaping our understanding of early childhood development. What makes recent findings so compelling are the enduring and largely irreversible ways in which social conditions and ways of relating are biologically woven into the brain in the first 1000 days. Most of adult mental ability is formed in the first three years of life, and about half of that before birth. There is overwhelming scientific evidence that the parent-child relationship, in particular responsive sensitive care in the early years of a child’s life, is critical to children’s development. The benefits of responsive caregiving are critical to healthy relationships later in life, in language skills and economic productivity in the adult years. We talk to experts in the field, neurologists, psychologists and early childhood development experts. We track the progress of babies in institutional care and travel with workers who educate women about their infants experience. The piece is intimate and accessible merging of science and relational care.
